title: How Munchausen Syndrome Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Munchausen syndrome, in which a psychologically driven person fakes or induces illness to receive medical care and sympathy, and its more harmful variant, Munchausen syndrome by proxy (factitious disorder imposed on another). They cover the history (Richard Asher naming it in the Lancet, Baron von Munchausen, Roy Meadows and the by-proxy term), risk factors, common deceptions (tampering with samples, self-injection, cut-and-smear), how doctors can spot it, and cases such as Julia "Casey" Swinson-style internet hoax, Mary Beth Tinning, Juanita Hoyt, and the David Southall controversy. The episode closes with a listener mail announcing a marriage proposal from listener Doug to his girlfriend Keina.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to faking illness
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk about manicures and nail biting, then mention The Sixth Sense and the Munchausen by proxy plot point, and introduce the term factitious disorder.

segments.title: Definition and internet-based Munchausen
segments.summary: The hosts define Munchausen syndrome as deliberately faking or inducing illness to get medical care and sympathy, and discuss Munchausen by internet, where people feign illness in online support groups.

segments.title: History and the Baron von Munchausen name
segments.summary: Richard Asher named the condition in the Lancet, after the eighteenth-century Baron von Munchausen, whose tales were later adapted by Terry Gilliam in a film starring Uma Thurman.

segments.title: Hypochondria and malingering distinctions
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish Munchausen from hypochondria, where people believe they are sick, and from malingering, which is faking illness for financial gain or to avoid work.

segments.title: Causes, risk factors and treatment
segments.summary: The disorder is described as psychological, linked to personality disorder, with risk factors such as early parental loss, childhood illness, and abuse. Treatment is approached like depression or anxiety, including cognitive behavioral therapy.

segments.title: Deception methods and warning signs for doctors
segments.summary: Patients use specific textbook symptoms, tamper with urine or thermometers, inject toxins, and seek many tests. Doctors can spot inconsistencies in medical history, eagerness for tests, and detailed hospital knowledge. A man who faked bereavement is described as an example.

segments.title: Dangers and cut-and-smear cases
segments.summary: The hosts discuss physical harm, suicide risk, amputations, and a case of a man who cut himself and smeared feces into wounds to cause infection, plus the wasted medical resources.

segments.title: Munchausen syndrome by proxy and controversies
segments.summary: Roy Meadows coined Munchausen by proxy and described cases of children made ill by a caregiver. David Southall's controversial surveillance videos and disputed accusations are discussed, along with concerns about Asperger's by proxy and cases such as Mary Beth Tinning and Juanita Hoyt.

segments.title: Notable Munchausen cases and pop culture references
segments.summary: The hosts mention William Palin, listed in the Guinness Book for numerous hospital treatments, the Casey Swinson online leukemia hoax, a mother-daughter double case, and references to Eminem and The X-Files.

segments.title: Listener mail: marriage proposal
segments.summary: Listener Doug from North Idaho plans to propose to his girlfriend Keina on her birthday, February 2, on the air.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the HowStuffWorks site and app and close the episode.
